query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy, brittle behavior at intermediate service temperatures emerges when the individual principal elements (e.g., Ni, Cr, Mn) rapidly segregate into the grain boundaries forming nanoclusters. These nanoclusters reduce grain boundary cohesion and promote intergranular crack initiation. By contrast, if pre-existing, embrittling-element–rich precipitates are introduced, they can absorb these elements and thereby maintain grain boundary integrity and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy (e.g., an equiatomic fcc CrMnFeCoNi alloy or a similar refractory HEA) with homogeneous elemental distribution and no pre-engineered secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled microstructural modification by engineering pre-existing, embrittling-element–rich precipitates (e.g., Cr-rich σ phases) at grain boundaries without changing the overall composition.
generation.conditions: Intermediate service temperatures (e.g., 450–700°C) under tensile or creep loading conditions, at strain rates relevant to engineering applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoclusters of principal elements (Ni, Cr, Mn) segregated at grain boundaries in the unmodified single-phase alloy, versus grain boundary regions decorated by stable precipitates in the engineered alloy.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, thermally activated diffusion causes rapid, localized segregation of certain principal elements to grain boundaries, forming nanoscale clusters that lower the cohesive strength of the boundary and facilitate intergranular fracture. In contrast, when grain boundaries are pre-decorated with stable Cr-rich precipitates, these sites capture embrittling elements, preventing their harmful segregation and preserving ductile grain boundary behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under tensile or creep testing at intermediate temperatures, the unmodified single-phase alloy will show a significant loss of ductility via intergranular brittle fracture, evidenced by low fracture strains and features of decohesion at the grain boundaries. The engineered alloy (with precipitates) will exhibit higher ductility and more ductile fracture morphologies because the precipitates redirect or absorb the segregation, mitigating the embrittlement process.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or homogenized single-phase HEA with uniform elemental distribution, which at room temperature exhibits high ductility and toughness but may suffer ductility loss at intermediate temperatures due to grain boundary decohesion.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis specifically applies to compositionally complex alloys under service conditions where temperature-induced diffusion and segregation are significant; it may not be relevant at very low temperatures (where diffusion is minimal) or at temperatures high enough to dissolve the nanoclusters or induce other phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of nanocluster formation, the critical grain boundary chemistry required for decohesion, and the quantitative differences in mechanical properties between the two microstructural states remain to be determined. The effectiveness of the precipitate engineering strategy in different HEA systems also requires further exploration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the same composition: (1) an as-homogenized single-phase HEA, and (2) an otherwise identical HEA processed to introduce stable, Cr-rich precipitates at grain boundaries (via controlled heat treatment with slower cooling rates). Subject both sets to standardized tensile (or creep) testing at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 600–700°C). Use complementary microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, APT) to assess grain boundary chemistry and fracture surface analysis to determine fracture mode.
measurements: Tensile ductility (elongation to failure) and yield strength at intermediate temperatures
Fracture surface morphology (intergranular versus transgranular features) via SEM/TEM
Grain boundary composition and nanocluster/precipitate distribution via atom probe tomography (APT) or energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the single-phase HEA without engineered precipitates does not exhibit a significant increase in intergranular cracking or loss of ductility relative to the precipitate-engineered HEA under the testing conditions, then the hypothesis that nanocluster-induced grain boundary decohesion is the dominant mechanism for brittle behavior would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time. This study, therefore, underscores the need for a better control of impurities in future development and application of RHEAs. In contrast to carbides and nitrides, intermetallic compound–induced embrittlement at room temperature can be relieved at high temperatures because plastic codeformation between these compounds and the matrix can reduce stress concentration and, thus, delay crack initiation (). A recent study of the single-phase fcc CoFeNi2V0.5Mo0.2 HEA demonstrated that the lack of Cr and Mn can evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures (). Therefore, we believe that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni system HEAs can embrittle GBs and, hence, lead to ductility loss with increasing deformation temperature. Note that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs also occurs at relatively low temperatures (<700°C), which accounts for ductility loss at intermediate temperatures. cited_evidence.text: Although the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is lower than the single-phase HEA at the testing temperature below 500°C, the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is greater than the single-phase HEA at 600° and 700°C. No intergranular embrittlement is observed. Figure 5 (B and C) shows the lateral surface in the vicinity of the fracture after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. Figure 5 (D and E) exhibits typical ductile dimples on fracture surfaces after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. In contrast to single-phase samples (Fig. 3D), the dual-phase sample has very few cracks near the lateral fracture surface. This suggests that the GB segregation engineering strategy via preexisting Cr-rich precipitates is effective to evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures in HEAs. This is because the embrittling elements—such as Cr, Mn, or Ni—can be absorbed by preexisting embrittling element–enriched precipitates at GBs, which only leads to the growth of precipitates rather than GB embrittlement.
